2637.dq: Kihm p.3: 'l’accent tonique (réalisé comme un ton haut) frappe le verbe à l’accompli (Man dé ‘J’ai mangé’), mais le pronom à l’inaccompli (Mán de ‘Je mangerai’)' — this concerns the clitic-pronoun + verb complex, not a citation-form word; Doneux's tone contrast is on the noun-class prefix (ba-yu vs bà-yu). Neither source states the domain of a word-stress rule because neither states such a rule.
2637.dloc: Kihm: p. 3 (A4 version), §2 'Le verbe et le complexe verbal', paragraph on the 1sg pronoun. || Doneux: p. 50, section '2. Une langue à double ou triple formation préfixielle'. || Doneux: p. 111, §6.2.3 'Tons' (the Persée 'fui' and 'par- 1ers' are scan errors for 'ful' and 'parlers').
2637.prule: No word-stress position rule is stated in any reachable source. Prominence is pitch-based: Doneux 1975 writes Manjaku with H vs L tone on noun-class prefixes (ba-yu H vs bà-yu L; 'ce qui est déterminant est le ton', p.50), says the language could equally be treated 'en termes d'accents' (L = unaccented), and in his typological summary (§6.2.3, p.111) places Manjaku NOT among the tone languages but in a third group 'avec résidus de système tonal' (with Fogny Jola); Kihm 2016 describes an 'accent tonique (réalisé comme un ton haut)' whose placement within the 1sg clitic + verb complex is grammatically contrastive (on the verb in the completive, on the pronoun in the incompletive) in dialects with a single 1sg pronoun man.

2637.exq_: Kihm p.3: 'certains dialectes opposent man (ACC) à me (INAC); pour ceux qui n’ont que man, la distinction est accentuelle' (the accentual contrast exists only in dialects with a single 1sg pronoun). No stress rule, so no exceptions to one.
2637.tone: Doneux 1975 (comparative noun-class study; Manjaku data from the Bok, Cur and Yu dialects) writes Manjaku with a two-way pitch contrast he calls 'ton haut' vs 'ton bas' (class prefixes ba-/bà-, ka-/kà-, p.50; 'la nasale syllabique est à ton haut' for the class-6 m- prefix in Bok, p.81) and explicitly says the same facts could be treated 'en termes d'accents' (low = unaccented). Crucially, in his summary typology of Atlantic tone (§6.2.3 'Tons', p.111) he distinguishes languages 'sans tons', 'avec tons' and a third group 'avec résidus de système tonal: manjaku, foni' — i.e. Manjaku is NOT classed as a full tone language but as one with residual tonal contrasts, which is what a pitch-accent (H-tone accent) reading amounts to. Kihm 2016 (fiche following Buis 1990's Bassarel transcription) accordingly calls the prominence 'l'accent tonique (réalisé comme un ton haut)', marked with an acute on the accented syllable (Man dé / Mán de); its placement within the 1sg subject-clitic + verb complex distinguishes completive from incompletive aspect. So the open descriptions agree on a high-pitch culminative prominence with grammatical (contrastive) placement and differ only in label (residual tone vs accent); neither gives a default position for word accent/stress. Kihm's 'Éléments de phonologie' (p.2) covers only vowels (ë, ä, e/ɛ, o/ɔ, length, weak nasalisation), d/r allophony and palatals. Mendes & Malherbe 2007 'Alphabet et prononciation' pp.9-11: letter values, ë 'très…

2638.dq: Automatic penult lengthening occurs phrase-finally in Manda, i.e. on the final antepenultimate position of a phonological phrase, rather than on a word. [...] Notice that the tones stay in their word-level position.
2638.dloc: Ch. 5 (grammar sketch), sec. 5.2.1.1 'Vowel length' pp. 46-47 and sec. 5.2.4 'Tone' pp. 54-55 with fn. 29
2638.prule: Restricted, predictable tone; no word stress. (Virtually) every word surfaces with a high tone placed near its right edge: nominals (incl. infinitives) carry H on antepenult+penult or on the penult alone (penult-only the commoner pattern; minimal pair kilólélo 'mirror' vs kilolélo 'dry season'); verb stems are toneless and the TAM conjugation assigns H on antepenult+penult or on the penult alone (stem-initial H when an object marker is inserted in APU+PU conjugations). Tone is obligatory and demarcative but not culminative (more than one H per word), so the author rejects both 'stress language' and Hyman's word-accent for Manda.
2638.srule: Not mentioned in Bernander 2017, ch. 5 secs. 5.2.1.1 (pp. 46-47) and 5.2.4 'Tone' (pp. 54-56) read in full: the source describes no word stress and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress (only H-tone positions and phrase-final penult lengthening).

2642.dq: Oft liegen die Silben eines Wortes anscheinend im Gleichgewicht oder es ist der Satz- bzw. Versrhythmus, der sie gliedert. So erklärt sich eine berechtigte Scheu des Sammlers ... bei jedem Wort den Akzent anzugeben, desgleichen das Schwanken meiner bald durch den Wort-, bald durch den Verston beeinflußten Akzentuierung oder ihr Ausbleiben.
2642.dloc: Prietze 1914, Einleitung, 'A. Die lautlichen Besonderheiten des Mangadialekts (M.)', point 5, pp. 135 (bottom)-136 (top)
2642.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Prietze 1914 (pre-tonological, one informant): the accent ('der Ton') in Manga tends to lie nearer the end of the word than in Koelle's Gazir Kanuri (búdu -> budú, tšéni -> žēní, kásagar -> kašágar, etc.), and certain suffixes (perfect/participial/conjunctional verb endings ži/či etc., 2sg imperative -e, plural -wa) are usually accented in Manga where Koelle/Barth have the accent before them; but the dynamic (stress) accent, even where it coincides with the musical (pitch) accent, is weak, the syllables of a word often sound level, and sentence/verse rhythm groups them, so he does not mark accent on every word. Modern Manga material (Jarrett 2007 dictionary) marks lexical tone on every syllable; Hutchison 1981 (Kanuri, Yerwa-based) states Kanuri is a tone language with no stress rule.
2642.srule: Not mentioned in Prietze 1914 (Einleitung A.5 and B, pp. 135-138 read): the source speaks only of where 'der Ton' tends to fall and says the dynamic accent is weak and the syllables of a word often seem in equilibrium; no secondary or rhythmic stresses are described. Later Manga material (Jarrett 2007) marks lexical tone only.

tn.quote: On trouve donc en kanouri les tons ponctuels (haut et bas) et les tons modulés (montant et descendant.) Les premiers ont une fonction distinctive et leur contexte d’occurrence ne connait pas de restriction. ... Le ton montant est moins fréquent que le ton descendant qui apparaît, en général, sur les syllabes finales. Le ton montant est obtenu par la jonction des deux tons bas et haut et le ton descendant par celle des deux tons haut et bas du moins en ce qui concerne les formes verbales. ... Nous avons ainsi les tons qui suivent: bas, haut, montant et descendant.
tn.translation: Thus one finds in Kanuri level tones (high and low) and contour tones (rising and falling). The former have a distinctive function and their context of occurrence is unrestricted. ... The rising tone is less frequent than the falling tone, which generally appears on final syllables. The rising tone is obtained by joining the two tones low and high, and the falling tone by joining the two tones high and low, at least as far as verb forms are concerned. ... We thus have the following tones: low, high, rising and falling.

In 1965 the conditions are written with /V: = any lengthened vowel except /a: and /V/ = any vowel except /a/ (p. 40), i.e. vowel length with a quality nuance (/a/, /a: weaker). Vowel length is phonemic (two lengtheners, /: raising and /;/ lowering, 1967 pp. 7 (a), 10; OPD 2007 lists long vowels aa ee ii oo uu êê ôô); 'Lengthened vowels do not occur word finally' (1965 fn. 6). Codas play no role in the 1967/2007 statements; the 1965 disyllable rule (a) lets a closed final syllable keep its stress against a short non-/a/ initial syllable, which the later statements drop.
2645.dflt: Words of 3+ syllables: antepenultimate primary stress with secondary stress on the ultimate syllable; disyllables: ultimate stress (1967 p. 3; 1965 p. 40 'a tendency to last and third to last stress in all words'). Four-syllable words 'do not follow this pattern as regularly'.
2645.prule: Default primary stress on the antepenultimate syllable (words of three or more syllables) and on the final syllable of disyllables; a preceding syllable with a long vowel attracts the stress away from the normally stressed syllable when that syllable has a short vowel (long /a: does so less reliably than other long vowels; OPD 2007: a syllable with a long non-central vowel is always stressed). Stress is weak (slight intensity, slight lengthening, slight high pitch) and non-contrastive apart from a few apparent pairs.
2645.srule: Secondary stress on the final (ultimate) syllable of words with antepenultimate primary stress ('mora'bir 'type of bird'); disyllables carry a single final stress; four-syllable words follow the pattern less regularly (Healey 1967 p. 3; restated in SIL-PNG OPD 2007 p. 3: 'antepenultimate stress with a secondary ultimate stress').

2646.dq: This paper investigates the acoustic correlates of word-level stress and phrase-level focus-related prominence in Mankiyali, a highly endangered Indo-Aryan language spoken in Northwest Pakistan that utilizes a weight-sensitive stress system. (Abstract, p. 289; cf. Paramore 2021 sec. 5.2 ‘Word Stress’, p. 43: ‘Primary stress placement in Mankiyali is sensitive to both syllable weight and the posit…
2646.dloc: Abstract, p. 289 (word-level stress vs phrase-level focus-related prominence); cf. Paramore 2021 sec. 5.2 'Word Stress', p. 43
2646.heavy: Three levels stated plainly: {CVː(C)} heaviest > {CVC(C)} middle > {CV} lightest (Paramore 2021 (3): VV(C)(C) > VC(C) > V). 2025 authors hypothesize five levels {CVːC} > {CVː} > {CVCC} > {CVC} > {CV} and report that duration results 'lend support to a five-way stress criterion'. Geminates absent from native words; onset complexity does not influence stress (thesis p. 43).
2646.dflt: penultimate syllable (when all syllables in the word are of the same weight; monosyllables trivially stressed)
2646.prule: Unbounded weight-sensitive stress: the heaviest syllable in the word takes primary stress regardless of position (including word-final); weight scale {CVː(C)} > {CVC(C)} > {CV} (Paramore 2021: VV(C)(C) > VC(C) > V), which the 2025 authors refine to a hypothesized five-level scale {CVːC} > {CVː} > {CVCC} > {CVC} > {CV}; when all syllables are of equal weight, stress is penultimate; when two or more syllables tie for heaviest, stress goes to the rightmost non-final one (a lone heaviest final syllable is stressed). Stress is not lexically contrastive.
2646.srule: Secondary stress on every long-vowel syllable CVː(C) that does not carry primary stress; short-vowel syllables (CV, CVC, CVCC) receive secondary stress only to avoid a lapse of two adjacent unstressed syllables (e.g. [ˈzaːn.ˌdaːk] 'child', [ˌkaː.ˈleː.zʌ] 'liver', [ˌkʌ.mʌ.ˈkʌ.lɑ] 'stupid', [ˈbʌŋg.su.ˌwɑ] 'buckle'). Paramore 2021 (sec. 5.2.2, p. 48) gives the same rule with a secondary-stress weight scale VV(C) > V(C)(C) and calls the secondary-stress findings preliminary.
2646.quote: Five syllable types in Mankiyali are relevant for determining stress placement: {CV, CVC, CVCC, CVː, CVːC}. Stress in Mankiyali, based on native-speaker judgments, is weight-sensitive and unbounded in that the heaviest syllable in a word attracts primary stress regardless of its position in the word. Moreover, Mankiyali possesses at least a ternary distinction in syllable weight, as demonstrated by the data in (1). (1) {CVː(C)} > {CVC(C)} > {CV} (Paramore, 2021: 44–47) ... When syllable weight is neutral in Mankiyali – where all syllables in a word are of the same weight – primary stress fall…
2646.loc: Sec. 2.4 'Mankiyali phonology', pp. 294-295 (quoted passage; uncertainty paragraph p. 295); five-level hypothesis (2) p. 296; sec. 5.4 'The Mankiyali stress criterion' pp. 320-321; conclusion sec. 6 p. 321 ('lend support to a five-way stress criterion'). Thesis: pp. 43-48 ('always attracts primary stress regardless of its location in the word or the morpheme in which it appears' p. 45); tone sec. 2.3 p. 25. Englert 2022 scan p. 3.
2646.idn: Mankiyali (thesis: language 'may have originally bore the name Tarawari'); single variety, no dialects named; data: Danna and Dameka villages near Oghi, Mansehra District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; JIPA recordings of 30 male speakers in summer 2022; thesis fieldwork with native speakers 2019-2021
2646.exq_: Paramore (2021) notes that the status of {CVCC} in relation to {CVC} and the status of {CVːC} in relation to {CVː} are uncertain in terms of weight distinctions for stress. Most speakers provide impressionistic judgments that primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable in words with two {CVː} …
2646.tone: Marginal binary lexical tone contrast (tonal vs atonal words, from loss of OIA voiced aspirates; low functional load; thesis sec. 2.3 pp. 25-26, Englert 2022 p. 3). Thesis p. 43: 'Contrastive tone exists in Mankiyali as briefly outlined in section 2 3 but the interaction between tone and stress are not explored in this thesis... no words that exhibit tone have been included in this section'. So stress rule holds for atonal words; tone-stress interaction unstudied.

2647.prule: No stress accent. Mano is a three-level tone language (L, M, H; marginal extra-high in ideophones/interjections; all nine two-tone contours on VV sequences; no downstep, no tone spreading). The only sub-word prosodic constituent is the 'metric foot' (V, CV(ŋ), CVV, CVCV(ŋ)), a domain of vowel harmony, intervocalic-consonant restrictions and grammatical tone replacement, not of prominence.

2647.quote: Mano has three level tones, low (kɛ̀ɛ̀ ‘year’), mid (kɛ̄ ‘in order to’), and high (kɛ́í ‘refuse’). 2647.tone: Three level tones L/M/H (kɛ̀ɛ̀ 'year', kɛ̄ 'in order to', kɛ́í 'refuse'); marginal extra-high in ideophones, expressive adverbs, interjections; TBU = vowel or syllabic nasal; all nine two-tone contours on VV; no downstep, no tonal spreading; grammatical tone replacement applies to one metric foot. 2650.heavy: 'non-CV syllables are always stressed' — i.e. CVV (a long vowel or two different vowels, stressed on the first) and CVN (nasal coda), the only non-CV syllable types; for primary stress: 'if the final syllable is CVC or CVV, the final syllable is stressed'. 2650.dflt: All-light words: stress on even-numbered syllables from the left (2nd, 4th...), final light syllable unstressed in every example; primary = rightmost beat: initial in the disyllable [ˈkẽj̃ẽ], penult in odd-syllable words ([ji.ˈmaː.ɗa], [ka.ˈnaː.wa], [ma.ˈna.ɾɨ], [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ]), antepenult in even-syllable words ([wa.ˈkaː.na.wa], [ɨ.ˈma.na.ɾɨ]) — the last contradicts the stated 'penultimate mora' default, which the author illustrates only with Wapishana.
2650.prule: As stated for both languages: intensity stress on the penultimate mora of the phonological word (final syllable if CVV/CVN, otherwise the penult). Mawayana-specific: rhythmic stress counted from the beginning of the word — every even-numbered CV syllable is stressed (with lengthening), non-CV (CVV, CVN) syllables are always stressed, prefixes count ([ka.ˈnaː.wa] vs [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa]); the author equates it with Cariban (Waiwai/Tiriyó) rhythmic stress and treats it as a borrowing. In his Mawayana examples the sole/primary stress is the rightmost rhythmic beat, which is the antepenult in even-parity all-light words ([wa.ˈkaː.na.wa], [ɨ.ˈma.na.ɾɨ]) — not the penult the joint statement predicts.
2650.srule: Rhythmic secondary stress on every even-numbered light (CV) syllable counted from the beginning of the phonological word (prefixes count, left to right); heavy syllables (CVV, CVN) are always stressed; the rightmost beat is primary, earlier beats secondary (/wa-katuku-sɨ/ [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ] 'our club'); a final light syllable is unstressed in the examples. 2652.dq: The phonetics of Margu are difficult, especially the frequent occurrence of γ and the irregularity of the tonic accent.
2652.prule: No rule stated. Capell's only prosodic remark is that the 'tonic accent' of Margu is irregular; no Margu form in the sketch (pp. 34-35) or in the Margu column of the vocabulary (p. 39) carries an accent mark. (The raised ticks on Buan and Gundangbon forms on p. 39, e.g. ŋa'bon, jala'bon, wa'wa', gu:', ŋu', dalugaṛa', are Capell's glottal-stop sign, not accent marks: part 1 of the survey explains the notation, 'the glottal stop is inserted between the two consonants as in yawar‘ra, I shall throw it away', p. 39 introduces the Gundangbon paradigm with 'It makes a much freer use of the glottal stop than any other form of that language', and several ticks are word-final, where an accent mark is impossible. Where Capell marks accent in this survey he uses an acute on the vowel, e.g. Burera 'angigélije anmuno' with '(accenting the first syllable in all cases)' in part 1; no Margu form carries an acute either.)

2654.prule: Word-level (lexical) stress falls on the root, by default on its first syllable: syllabic trochees built left to right with End Rule Left; quantity-insensitive; suffixes are subordinated to the root stress (initial stress for the ordinary word).

In words (or prosodic groups) of five or more syllables a second, rhythmic stress falls on the 4th syllable: a syllabic trochee built left to right at the end of the word, non-adjacent to the root foot (one syllable skipped, no degenerate feet), Costa's 'alternância ternária iterativa' (level 2, 'regulação rítmica/acento frasal', applying post-lexically even to a single long word). By End Rule Right on the phrase layer this rhythmic stress is transcribed as the stronger one (»»), the root stress as weaker (»): »aNtsa-ma-ʃ»»ta-sɨ 'pouquinho', nu»ku-ka»»ɾaN-va-ya, »vatʃi-naN»»naN-vai-vu. In compounds the second root's stress surfaces only in isolation/slow speech; under clash the weaker stress deletes.

2656.tone: Bostoen 2007 says nothing about stress or accent. It presents all Kwamashi lexical items with H (acute) and L (grave) tone marks from the author's 2005 field notes and states that the underlying tone scheme of Kwamashi nouns is a regular reflex of Proto-Bantu *LH / *HH patterns, i.e. Kwamashi has lexical tone. No statement about penultimate lengthening, stress placement, or the absence of stress. The areal remark in Kashoki & Mann 1978:70 ('In Zambian languages... syllables are more or less evenly stressed... stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning') is not made for Mashi by name and is not used as evidence here.

2657.dq: Stress seems to be assigned from the right margin of the word following the non-high vowel > high vowel weighting, and then the finer gradations of weighting. Apparently the finer gradations of weight can be overruled by sentence initial and sentence final intonation. Thus sentence internally /e.ˈnan/ ‘that’ was recorded, but sentence initially it was /ˈe.nan/.
2657.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.10 Stress, pp. 31-36; quoted sentences from p. 32, p. 33 ranking, p. 35 bullets, p. 36 summary; Tables 6-7 p. 33; example sets p. 34; also abstract p. iii and sec. 1.4.1.2
2657.heavy: Not rime weight. 'syllables containing non-high vowels are ranked as heavier than those containing high vowels' (p. 33), refined by Tables 6-7 to non-high (a > e, o) > high (i, u > ə); stressed 'regardless of syllable shape or whether the syllable is penultimate or ultimate' (p. 32); the author explicitly rejects his initial coda-based analysis ('closed syllables attracting stress word finally. This would have been a mistake', p. 32); /ə/ 'does not carry stress regardless of position (0/11)' (p. 33). Compared by the author to Kara and Kobon and to de Lacy's (2007) vowel sonority hierarchy.
2657.dflt: When the last two syllables have identical vowels (equal weight): penultimate stress with alternate preceding syllables also stressed ('impressionistically 44/45 CVCV# forms and 91/98 CVCVC# forms are stressed on the penultimate syllable'). When the final two syllables have merely similar weights (e.g. a vs e, i vs u) the same speaker may stress either (/ˈxa.ᵐbat/ ~ /xa.ˈᵐbat/, /ˈa.le/ ~ /a.ˈle/).
2657.prule: Stress is assigned by vowel quality (which the author calls syllable weight), scanning from the right edge of the word: the rightmost syllable whose nucleus is highest on the scale non-high (a > e, o) > high (i, u > ə) takes primary stress, 'regardless of syllable shape' (codas irrelevant; /ə/ never stressed, 0/11). When the last two syllables have identical vowels (equal weight) stress defaults to the penult with alternate preceding syllables also stressed (44/45 CVCV#, 91/98 CVCVC#). Examples p. 34: /ˈsa.rex/ 'deep', /ˈa.kis/ 'always' vs /pe.ˈlan/ 'tomorrow', /si.ˈpa/ 'thanks', /mə.ˈxat/ 'up'; /ˈᵐbe.xi/ 'shark', /ˈlo.tu/ 'worship' vs /ᵐbu.ˈse/ 'grass skirt', /ni.ˈno/ 'yesterday'; /mə.ˈtu/ 'coconut'; /ˈmɑ.pʷir.xət/ 'small piece of s.t.' (antepenult /a/ wins over penult /i/ and final /ə/).
2657.srule: Rightmost stressed syllable = primary; any other stressed syllable = secondary (acoustically not consistently weaker than the primary). Secondary stresses fall on other weighted (non-high-vowel) syllables to the left of the primary (/ˌa.so.ˈan/, /ˌmʷor.ˈmʷo.ri/, /ˌna.ˌsor.xu.su.ri.ˈan/ 'on each of the non-high vowels') and otherwise on alternate preceding syllables ('penultimate stress with alternate preceding syllables also being stressed' when all else is equal; /ˌna.ᵐbu.ˌnu.si.ˈan/ 'the first weighted syllable then every second preceding syllable'). Hedged by the author ('seems', 'appears').

2660.prule: Lexically specified stress parity: every root is listed as odd-stressed (syllables 1, 3, 5... counting from the left carry stress) or even-stressed (syllables 2, 4, 6...); stress then alternates rigidly through the whole phonological word regardless of what suffixes/enclitics follow ('once you know whether the first syllable is stressed or not, you know which other syllables in the word will carry stress', p. 165). Quantity-insensitive. Minimal pairs exist ([tʃú.wa] 'heat up' vs [tʃu.wá] 'miss'; [á.bi] 'presently/still' vs [a.bí] '4 Absolutive'). Even-stressed roots are the majority (3-4x more common); Spanish loans are 'sometimes' and lexicalized roots 'may' be adapted to the even-stressed pattern (p. 184). Phonetic correlates: vowel length and pitch.
2660.srule: Every other syllable of the phonological word is stressed, on the root's lexical odd/even parity counted from the left, quantity-insensitively; the stresses are unranked: 'The rightmost word-level stress seems to be the strongest, but not very noticeably so..., so I do not distinguish between primary and secondary word-level stress' (p. 185).

2662.prule: No word stress. Mawa is a tone language: three surface pitch levels H/M/L reduce to two contrasting underlying tones M and L with the syllable as tone-bearing unit (H a conditioned realization, chiefly on grammatical morphemes and word-finally after M; 'superhigh' at a deeper level). Prominence 'is achieved solely by means of pitch (or tone) differences'. Under the author's trial accentual reinterpretation the 'accent' = the M-toned syllable, whose position is lexically contrastive in nouns (L(L) = no accent; M(M), LM, MH) and a two-way lexical class in verbs (M = accented, L = unaccented); grammatical morphemes (infinitive -Vng, past, possessive person markers, oblique -o/-ro) contribute accents that cancel clashing lexical ones. No fixed position is stated; syllable weight plays no role.

2662.tone: Whole paper is on the suprasegmental system. Sec. 4.1 (tonal analysis, p. 12): 'Mawa has two contrasting tones, M and L... the syllable is the tone-bearing unit' (fn. 5: at a deeper level simply High and Low, the surface H a superhigh). Sec. 4.2 (accentual analysis, pp. 13-15) is explicitly about stress/accent: prominence 'achieved solely by means of pitch (or tone) differences'; accent = the M-toned syllable; but L-class verbs and L(L) nouns would be accentless (violating one-accent-per-word) and disyllabic nouns would place the accent 'in three contrastingly different places'; tone polarity and neutralization under suffixation (past, possessive, infinitive, oblique) read as accent-clash cancellation; 'no word will have more than one independent M tone (that is, more than one accent)'. Sec. 4.3 (p. 16): 'Mawa displays characteristics of a tone system and of an accentual system, although neither framework as conceived at present is able to capture all the relevant facts'. No stress independent of pitch; no fixed stress position; no intensity or length correlate claimed. Phrase-final H realized as a fall (p. 1); postlexical Rule (11) handles the L/H alternation within and across words.

tn.quote: For the tonal analysis, it can be assumed that Mawa has two contrasting tones, M and L5, and that the syllable is the tone-bearing unit. ...
